history_title: Native objections, patents and estate law
history_content:
A homeland across beach and bay

Fire Island is the long barrier beach between the Atlantic Ocean and Long Island's south-shore bays. These waters connected communities rather than separating them. Unkechaug, Secatogue and Shinnecock people used the beach and surrounding waters for food, seasonal activity and cultural life long before English estates or summer resorts. Those relationships continue. Poospatuck, the Unkechaug community on the mainland, remains connected to the bay and Fire Island. Native American Heritage at Fire Island National Seashore

The Native objection inside the ownership record

Colonial documents did not tell one uncontested story. The National Park Service's 1979 historic study reports that, in a 1693 letter, Sachem Tobagus denied selling South Beach to Brookhaven and said that his signature on an earlier document had been forged. This is an allegation recorded in the study's account of the letter; it matters because it challenges the assumption that a colonial claim necessarily rested on an agreed Native sale. Historic Resource Study: Fire Island National Seashore, Long Island, N.Y.

Who claimed authority to grant the beach?

English governor Thomas Dongan's 1686 Brookhaven patent excepted Native land south of the town's limits that had not been purchased. Another Dongan grant, to William Nicoll in 1688, did not include Great South Beach. These distinctions gave competing English claimants room to pursue new grants; they also show why a town patent cannot simply be read as proof that every Native interest had ended. Historic Resource Study: Fire Island National Seashore, Long Island, N.Y.

In 1693, English governor Benjamin Fletcher granted William “Tangier” Smith a claim that included Great South Beach from Huntington East Gut, identified in the study with Fire Island Inlet, east to Cupswauge at Southampton's western bounds. It also included bay rights. Smith sought this grant after acquiring lands within Brookhaven's claimed boundaries. The study distinguishes the governor's patent from a further Native deed dated April 10, 1694. They were different instruments, issued through different relationships and assertions of authority. Historic Resource Study: Fire Island National Seashore, Long Island, N.Y.

Turning a coastal homeland into inheritable property

After Smith died in 1704, the beach became part of his sons' inheritance. The estate used English legal rules that could restrict property to a specified line of heirs. Henry Smith and his eldest son William later used a court procedure called common recovery to remove that restriction and divide their interests. This was legal machinery for passing and rearranging an estate; those later family transactions do not establish what Native people had agreed to give up. Historic Resource Study: Fire Island National Seashore, Long Island, N.Y.

Here the difference between relationships to land and a private title becomes concrete. The record concerns not only sand, but access to waters, food and a continuing homeland. A governor's grant and an estate's succession could make control transferable within colonial law while Native people continued to assert relationships and objections. The historical evidence supports that tension; it does not let us assign one identical understanding of every deed to all Native signatories. Native American Heritage at Fire Island National Seashore; Historic Resource Study: Fire Island National Seashore, Long Island, N.Y.

A future beyond a record of loss

Native life did not end when an English estate appeared on paper. The National Park Service recognizes continuing Indigenous stewardship and the enduring Unkechaug community at Poospatuck. Understanding this beach therefore requires both the colonial ownership record and living Native relationships to it. Native American Heritage at Fire Island National Seashore

Public conservation and LandBack ask different questions. Protecting a beach from development does not by itself return land or decision-making authority to a Native nation. The map's LandBack section explains examples of Indigenous-led stewardship and return. For Fire Island, a useful starting question is whose knowledge, access and authority shape decisions about this living coastal homeland.

Continue with the Unkechaug community at Poospatuck and Brookhaven’s mainland claims and retained Native land.
whereintheworld_content: This outline follows the modern Fire Island barrier from Fire Island Inlet to Moriches Inlet. It is an area for reading the history, not a surveyed reconstruction of the 1693 grant. Shores and inlets have changed, and the historical Great South Beach claim extended toward Cupswauge. Smaller bay islands called Fire Islands in some colonial records are not interchangeable with the outer beach. The outline does not map every bay right or imply that all Native relationships ended in 1693.
